To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the adverse influence of maternal tobacco use on birth outcomes appears to be modiated by increasing maternal body weight.
the effect of smoking on birth weight is reduced with increasing BMI.
maternal smoking during pregnancy has a negative effect on birth weight and that the effect of smoking is reduced in overweight and obese women.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the differential effect of smoking on birth weight, and how that relationship may be affected by the mother's weight.
the interaction between smoking and body mass index (as measured by the body mass index).
the interaction between maternal weight and tobacco exposure, and the effects of that interaction on birth weight.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
maternal BMI and tobacco exposure are independent risk factors for low birth weight, and the effect on birth weight of smoking is reduced with increasing maternal weight.
the adverse effect of tobacco use on low birth weight is greater in leaner women, while the effect is reduced in women of high BMI.
the adverse effect of smoking during pregnancy on birth weight is lessened as maternal body weight increases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the adverse influence of smoking on birth weight appears greatest for leaner women and least for those with high BMI, with a significant decline between these two groups.
the effects of tobacco exposure on birth weight are not uniform across all women, but rather are dependent on maternal weight.
the adverse effects of tobacco use on fetal weight appear to be modulated in a positive manner by increased maternal body weight.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of tobacco use on fetal growth may be lessened for women with higher BMI.
, in the presence of high BMI, tobacco use has less of an adverse effect on birth weight.
the effect of smoking on birth weight is not linear, but is modified by maternal body weight.
